div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: —A Hall at the Country Seat of Sir Oswin Mortland.
A loud knocking at the Gate.
Enter Mrs. Sarah Mortland, followed by a Servant.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Tell the coachman I shan't want the carriage this morning.—And observe, if my brother should ask for me, I am gone to take a walk in the beech grove.

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: Yes, ma'am.

div.stage: Enter another Servant (in a great hurry).

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: Ma'am, there's a young lady in a post chaise just stopt at the gate, and says she must see you.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: A young lady! Must see me!—Who is she? What is her name?

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: I asked her name, ma'am, but she refused to tell it.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Refused to send me her name! Then pray inform her that I am not at home—tell her I'm busy —I will be seen by no one.

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: I told her, ma'am, that you were busy, and that you had company, and that you were not at home; but she says she is come post more than twenty miles on purpose to pay you a visit, and cannot return without seeing you.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: What an impertinent!—Come post!—show her in—how extremely ridiculous and ill bred—

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: Here she is, ma'am.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: My dear Miss ---! It is Miss ---, the young lady I met at Beverly—is it not?—What in the name of wonder—

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Oh, Mrs. Sarah Mortland! Oh, madam, pity and forgive me!—forgive this intrusion, and pity the cause of it.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: My dear, I must forgive all you do.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I thought so, madam—I hoped you would forgive me, when I resolved to take this liberty. The kindness, the partiality you showed towards me, the very first time I was in your company—

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: And which was the last, I believe, my dear; for I think I never saw you but once in my life.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: No, madam; at Mrs. Brian's ball, when you were there at Beverly races. But that once you praised my dancing, my singing, my conversation! You said, if you remember, that you wished you had just such a young companion as I was—you told me you should be glad to see me at any time—and so I am come.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Well!—and I am glad, very glad to see you.—I don't say I'm not.—Only a little surprised, my dear, that you did not wait for a more formal invitation.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: What it wanted in form, you made up with earnestness.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: And I then, at that time, felt all the ardour I expressed, But, my dear, are you come by yourself?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Did you wish me to bring any body else?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I thought you would not—so I flew to you all alone, in my distress.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: But what distress? And why are you in tears? I hope you have not run away from your friends?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I have no friend but you.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Hem! hem!
But, my dear, tell me what is all this about? And why
have I the pleasure of seeing you here?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: You know that I am an orphan!

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Yes, that I was told—but I really forget your name.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: My Christian name is Hester—and when I am called by any other, it is that of my guardian, with whom I have lived from my infancy—Mr. Ashdale.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Hester Ashdale.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: For my guardian never speaks of my own family but with reproach; has seldom permitted me to ask him any questions concerning them; and, indeed, has ever treated me with cruelty!

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: We all have our trials, and we ought all to submit to them.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: But mayn't we run away from them?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Not always. Pray, when did you leave your guardian's house?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: This very morning.—This very morning I was to have been married—and they are now all waiting for me at the church, or by this time gone home to a very uncomfortable dinner without me.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Without the bride!—Was there ever!—

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: But, if you knew the intended bridegroom, you would not wonder.—He is so odious to me, that I had rather stay with you by half; and be your companion or servant.—I'll read—I'll sing—I'll work—I'll do every thing to please you.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: But, my dear, this house I cannot call my own. —It is, in fact, my brother's, Sir Oswin Mortland's. —As I live entirely in the country, he suffers me to pass for the mistress of it, but at present, he's down here himself; and though much younger than I am, yet he is so much richer and wiser than I am, that he commands me in every thing.—Indeed, such is his temper, he will always be lord and master of every place into which he condescends to enter; and he hates intruders —strangers—strange ladies in particular.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Then why did you invite me to come?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: I invited you, but I did not fix the time.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: No, madam—but I thought I might.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Then, your indiscretion in quitting your guardian's house, and your intended husband!—Why did you give your consent to marry?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I was in such fear of my guardian's anger, and his wife's peevishness.—I had no sense, no skill, no argument to answer all they said to prevail on me!—It was, besides, so ill bred to tell a gentleman, that I could not love him! that I could not bear to live with him! that he was disagreeable to me!

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: So, then, you consented without any apparent reluctance!

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I am sure I looked reluctantly: but I was obliged to say yes, to all they asked of me.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Then you should have kept your word.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Indeed and so I intended till it came to the very last—then I planned my escape. Did you never resolve on a thing and think you would do it whatever it cost you: then, just on the point when it was to be done, find your heart sink, and all your resolutions turn to nothing?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: It must have been some very shocking husband they designed for you, to give you such an aversion!

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Oh he was not so very bad neither!—I dare say you would have had no objection to marry him: but I always said to myself—“I think a wedding is so pleasant;—the bells ring so sweetly; the bride and the bridemaids look so nice; and every one so joyful—that I never will marry, unless I can be joyful too.”

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: But when you return to your guardians, what do you think they will say to you for this conduct?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I never mean to return madam; and by the time I have lived a week or two here, perhaps you may never wish me to go back.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: “A week or two”—“never go back”—I must instantly acquaint Sir Oswin with this visit, and obtain his permission before I can venture to say you shall stay here even an hour or two.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Then dear, dear Mrs. Sarah Mortland, as this Sir Oswin is a cross ill-natured man, don't say I ran away just as I was going to be married: it may make him think me to blame.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Tell him that! Not for the universe! If I were, he would not merely turn you out of his house, but me, for suffering you to come into it.—Step into that room while I go to him.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Oh Madam, rash as I may seem in having ventured hither, my heart has beat with fear, more than with hope. Pity me as a stranger in this house, and reflect that on my reception here, depends all my future prospects.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: I vow she has put me in such a fright! What can I say to Sir Oswin? I did ask her to come, and see me to be sure; and it would be uncharitable to turn her out—and yet it was equally uncharitable to come on such an invitation.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Lord Danberry raps at the door twice.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Who's there?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Nephew! nephew!—I beg your pardon—I know you don't like to be interrupted in your studies.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Yet my friends generally break in upon me at those very times my lord,—and tell me—“they know they are disobliging me”—by way of apology.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Well, but you will excuse me—you'll excuse me I fear, sooner than my errand, for that I know you'll be displeased with.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Another apology!

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Well, nephew, it does not signify,—but I must ask you again and again,—will you suffer my fine estate and our old title to go to a mere stranger? —This, you know, must be the case, if you resolve to continue a bachelor:—The thought of it embitters my life.—Consider, Sir Oswin, marriage as I have often told you, is a duty every man in your situation owes to his family, to society, to—

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Well, well, I grant it, my dear uncle,—and as my temper cannot bear continual irritation, I shall comply with your request to get rid of it for ever. —I will marry, to put an end to all your anxieties, though I had rather—

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: —Thank you, my dear nephew, for this hearty promise: you have made me happy.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: And myself miserable.—I never thought of becoming a husband. I never intended to be a husband. Marriage will interfere with my pursuits, my studies, my—

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: You will like the marriage state better than you expect.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Why, my Lord, I shall, at least, meet with no disappointments in it. For I do, with certainty, expect that it will progressively destroy every comfort of my life; and I shall fortify myself against their total extinction.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: I own the prospect for a married man is not very bright just at this precise period.—But, without dwelling on your character as a husband, consider the happiness you may enjoy as a parent. Reflect upon a son and heir!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I can feel no happiness in contemplating what does not exist.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: But I can. I can experience the highest gratification in foreseeing that now a son of yours will inherit my title and estates when I am laid low: for, by the course of years, I have but a short time to live.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: So my marriage, which will inevitably rob me of every enjoyment I possess, is to accommodate two nonentities; one of whom will be gone out of the world, and the other not come into it!

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Still, there is a being in full existence, in the bloom of life, to whom your marriage will give high delight. The lady, with whom I mean you to marry—Lady Susan Courtly.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Lady Susan Courtly!

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Yes;—and who, I believe, is as much in love with you—
sp.stage: (Sir Oswin goes to him, and looks him in the face with a smile.)

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: My Lord—I am between thirty and forty years of age.—I have lived in the world, at least half those years, an observer.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: I know you have.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: And do you talk to me of being in love?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Not you, but the lady. The lady, I say, is in love.—Lady Susan.
sp.stage: (Sir Oswin, after looking steadfastly on him, turns away.)

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Psha! psha! psha!

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: She fancies she is.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: But she won't make me fancy she is.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: I know you don't believe there is such a thing, as what is usually meant by the word love. But don't you think there may be such a thing as a good wife?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Yes, faith, I think there may.—I think, possibly, there may.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: And why shou'dn't she fall to your share?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: O, my Lord,—It would be unconscionable in me to expect it. I can't hope to monopolize rarity.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Ay, you are jocose; you make free with your old uncle.
sp.stage: (Sir Oswin takes his hand kindly, as if apologising.)
sp.p: And now I'll tell you how your old uncle has made free with you. I have brought down Lady Susan Courtly to my house, here in the country—on this very spot—in the firm persuasion that you are smitten with her charms: but that you are too grave, too reserved, too consequential, think too much of your own importance and perfections, to ask a favour, even of a lady.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Why, my Lord!—

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: So, to save your dignity from the humiliation of sighing and kneeling, I have in your name solicited her hand in marriage.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: My Lord, I should be very sorry you appear'd ridiculous in this affair.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: I knew you would—you always were careful of my reputation, and therefore I knew you would acknowledge as yours, every syllable I have said in your name.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Here's the beginning of matrimony! Always false foundations!

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: But tell me? Don't you like Lady Susan now, as well as you do any other woman?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Quite as well—she is the same to me as her whole sex. I have no partiality to any one, nor dislike to any one, except as a wife.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Human foresight is truly exemplified in me! My pride has been to make you a learned man, a man of erudition. And what is my reward? You love nothing but books.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Yes, my Lord, I love the whole human race— and I love my books, because they have taught me to do so.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Can you boldly repeat that you love all mankind? There is one man whom I am sure you exclude from the rest.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: You mean the state delinquent, Lavensforth— a man who has attempted my life.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Not directly.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Pardon me, my Lord;—his challenge was a direct attempt: and though the laws interfered, and disappointed that hope of his revenge; yet I have reason to believe he did not give up his designs against me, even when he left the kingdom.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: That is now full thirteen years ago; and if he be still living—

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: —He is rancorous still: his rage was of no transient nature.—Yes, I own I do not love the man who can bear malice for an act of justice; or could impute to my clear motives in his impeachment, any other end than the public good.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: But the public took such interest in the cause. —Your triumph was so popular, and his defeat so—

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Ay, that defeat, as well as his consequent punishment, may have been too severe: for though his sentence reached only to a fine, yet ultimately it proved so heavy, that, in effect, it caused his exile.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: So much the better.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: And, after all—though one may be ruined, and another raised to fame by rigorous prosecution of the faults of office; yet, in the candid estimate of man's imperfections and man's virtues, the accuser is seldom entirely right, nor the accused totally wrong.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Why I never heard you talk thus before—nor would I have the world hear you now. You did not speak thus on Lavensforth's impeachment.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: No!—Youthful ardour made me then pronounce with decision. Years of studious application, and more matur'd experience have lessened my confidence in my own opinions.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Ay, you are in an ill humour now, and so you'll contradict every thing I assert. I am glad, however, to hear you speak so diffidently of your own judgment, for then you can the better rely on mine, and keep the promise you have made me.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Yes—my Lord—as I have said; I'll marry in obedience to your will—I'll keep my word.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: But now when? When will you fix the happy day? When will you marry?
Why as you have no great inclination to the business, don't delay —marry soon—as you don't like it, get it over at once.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: “Get it over?” Why it's to last for life.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Not always. There is such a thing as benefit of survivorship.
sp.stage: (Mrs. Sarah Mortland raps at the Library door.)

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Come in.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Then I'll go. And I'll go out at this door that I mayn't meet your company.
And much obliged to you, my dear nephew, I am for all you have promised—I'm sure Lady Susan will be—
sp.stage: (She raps again at the library door.)

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Come in.—

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: To tell you the truth, I am half afraid to come in.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Because I have told you a thousand times, you may command any part of my day but this.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: I beg pardon,—I'll tell her you'll call on her today, or to-morrow morning.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: My Lord!—You need not be afraid, however, sister; for, at present, your intrusion is not unwelcome.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Nay, I am not so much alarmed at my intrusion, as at my errand: for I am come to tell you something you won't like.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: More things I don't like, and more apologies! Why, then
you have chosen a bad time for your bad news, for I am in a very ill temper.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: The reason I came now was—that you might not be more offended at dinner time, by meeting a stranger at table. It is hard I can't make you love strangers!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Why won't you be content with my loving you?—Why won't you be contented with my loving all my old, troublesome, tiresome friends? If I loved the company of every idle stranger, ten to one I could not endure yours.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: That I would pardon, could I once see you enjoy society like other people. But, I believe, I shall soon begin to think you have taken two of the monastic vows; that of seclusion, and the other against marriage.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: In the latter, I shall at least boast your example.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: You are mistaken.—I never made a vow against marriage. It was the men, I believe, who vowed never to ask me the question. Let me tell you, brother, there is a great deal of difference in sentiment, between a single man of a certain age, and a single woman of a certain age. The one does not marry because he won't:—the other, because she can't.—But we'll not talk of these things now.—
It's only a pretty girl is to dine with us to day.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: What have I to do with pretty girls?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: I said so,—I thought so;—I knew you would not like her coming.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Then why did you invite her?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: I only invited her in the usual complimentary way; told her I should be glad to see her at any time; begged she would make this house her home if she came into this part of the world. She lived twenty miles off, and I never imagin'd—

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Oh that every ostentatious invitation, was just so received!

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: I own that I did wrong; and therefore have taken her in for a few days.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: “A few days”—For yourself, you are justly repaid: for me, I will have no annoyance from your visitors. I shall set off for London tomorrow morning.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Nay, nay—why, she won't be in your way— You will never see her, but at breakfast, dinner, and supper.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: So,—she's only to torment me from morning till night.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: —One of the most beautiful young women!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: What's her beauty to me?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: An orphan—without parents to protect her— without a single relation, that she knows, on earth—
Has been so cruelly used! —You won't go to town, will you?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: —If you had seen how the poor creature wept when she arrived, and hung on me for pity!— You'll dine with us to-day?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Perhaps I may.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: —And you'll behave civilly to this poor girl? I'll tell you who she is.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: No, no; I don't want to know who she is.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: —Her distress is so great!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Why then I don't care who she is.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Well, brother, now, I suppose, I have your leave to go?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: How can you doubt it?

div.stage: (The Scene closes on Sir Oswin writing.)

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: I tell you, I'm sure he will see me. Tell him, I come on very particular business.

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: Mr. Willowear.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Mr. Willowear, my old acquaintance and school-fellow! —Shew him in.
I thought he was too fond of London, ever to be seen out of St. James's-street.
What can be his particular business with me?

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Sir Oswin, I have taken this liberty—

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Mr. Willowear, you tremble!—What causes this agitation?

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: The cause is, I am in a passion—and I can hardly tell my story for anger.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: You are not angry with me, I hope.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: No; heaven forbid!—But you will excuse me, if I say, I am offended with some part of your family.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Shew me in what any of them have used you ill, and you shall have instant redress. Pray sit down.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: I am sorry to name a lady of your family—a lady, whom I have not the honour of knowing— your sister.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: My sister!

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Yes; and another Lady has used me worse, and has flown to her for protection.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I have just been quarrelling with my sister, for taking a young woman into the house.—Does she belong to you?

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: She was within—To tell you the whole story, Sir Oswin: the other day I fell in love.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: A beautiful girl!—You might have done the same thing.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: No, no;—Ha, ha, ha! I beg your pardon.— Proceed with your story—Ha, ha, ha! you know I was never in love.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: But can you pretend to say, you never shall!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Yes, I can.—But proceed.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: A little, friendless girl! hardly any body knew: who—brought up by the apothecary of our village. She caught my eye—her simple manners won my heart. I admire simplicity, of all female qualities.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: So do I.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: I grew tired of leading a batchelor's life. I had seen you, Sir Oswin, for instance, often out of temper—crabbed and rugged. No other fault, you know, ever laid to your charge, than being a little sullen, morose, and rather imperious. But all this, the women said, was merely for want of a wife.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: “The women said!”—My dear sir, pray go on with your story. Does this young lady, in my house, belong to you?

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Yes—no—she was very near it, though—I won't say how very, very near it; for then you'll laugh again, and with some reason.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: What! I suppose, the ring bought.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: The book opened—when she took it in her head to run away.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Monstrous! abominable! not to be borne! She has imposed on my sister with some piteous tale.—But she sha'n't remain here a moment longer.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: I thought you would not suffer it.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Certainly not.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: How she contriv'd to have every thing ready to make her escape, no one can guess. But, instead of meeting me in the church, where I was waiting with a few friends, impatient for her coming, she slipt from her bridemaids into a post-chaise, and drove to your house, where I have traced her.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Who's there?
Tell my sister, I desire to see her, and the Lady (the young woman, who came hither this morning) in the parlour by the saloon immediately.
Depend upon it, she shall leave this house instantly, or give me the very best reasons why she shou'd not.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: She can give you none—after encouraging my addresses, accepting my presents—for I gave her trinkets in abundance, and a diamond ring of great value,—In a word, I, myself, am the only gift she ever refused.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: And, does she expect a refuge under my roof thus charged with robbery?

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: The goods are upon her, I dare say. But, after all, I wou'd rather have her back, than my property. She is more precious to me than my diamond.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: “Precious! Have her back!” Wish to have such a woman for a wife!

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Very true—I am wrong, I own—but, love! love! —Notwithstanding your sneer, Sir Oswin, love is ev'ry thing.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: No, 'tis nothing—a whim—a fancy, conceived by the infirmity of youth, or of age.—At seventeen or seventy, the infatuation is excusable,—but, at your time of life, and mine, Oh! it sinks the man into the boy, or dotard.—But, come, I'll shew you to my plantations, where you may amuse yourself, while I talk to these women—and, depend on my settling this business with as much care and concern for your welfare, as if I had your faith in the omnipotence of love.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter Mrs. Sarah Mortland and Hester.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Come, come—don't tremble thus—don't cry thus—don't be thus alarm'd.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Is not Sir Oswin coming to talk to me? perhaps to put himself in a passion—to turn me out of the only place I have to shelter me.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: He has merely sent word, he wishes to speak to us; and will most likely be as angry with me as with you.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: You are accustomed to his sternness.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Stern as he is, he has the best of hearts to those who deserve his kindness.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: But I know myself undeserving.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: And your disappointed lover, who is certainly come to Sir Oswin on your account, has, no doubt, painted your conduct in the very worst colours.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Dear madam, let me run away again—suffer me to go before Sir Oswin comes, and save me the disgrace of being turned out.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: No; I should be turned out myself, if I were to connive at your escape. There is one circumstance, however, relative to you, that I do wish concealed from my brother, because it increases the peril of your situation.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Dear Madam what is it?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Your guardian has sent me a letter by this Mr. Willowear, in which he informs me, that your real name is Lavensforth, and that you are the daughter, the only child of Sir Oswin's inveterate enemy.—By this intelligence your guardian conceives you will immediately be restored to him, as my brother, under such circumstances, would not suffer you to remain a moment longer here.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Yes, Madam, I am the child of an unfortunate man, whose name I never heard without upbraidings. I knew he had many enemies, and for that reason I was denied my right to be called by his name: but I did not know that Sir Oswin was his particular foe.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Yes; and tho', possibly, both of them good men, peculiar occurrences in the earlier part of their lives, when Sir Oswin was very young indeed, made them the bitterest enemies.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Oh, then, my dear, dear, Madam, do not tell Sir Oswin who I am, 'till I am gone away—Indeed, I'll go the moment he has seen me. But if you please, I had rather go now.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Do you think Mr. Willowear has told my brother who you are?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: No—I am sure Mr. Willowear does not know himself: for my guardian, fearing he might object to my father's misfortunes, always charged me to conceal my real name from him.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Then, I promise you, my brother shall never know it from me. Your guardian, indeed, enjoins me silence to all but Sir Oswin; of course, he can hear it no other way.—And this secret of your birth, Mr. Ashdale adds in his letter, was in consequence of a promise your father extorted, when he left you to his care.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: My father made him promise also, he would treat me with kindness—but in that, he never kept his word.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: You remember your father then?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Yes, yes; I shall always remember him; though, I fear, he has forgot me.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: You think, he is still living then?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I hope so! but, for these two last years, no letter —no—

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Hush! hush! Sir Oswin.

div.stage: Enter Sir Oswin—he passes his Sister, and stands between her and Hester.

sp.speaker: Sir Oswin.
sp.p: My business with you, Madam, and with this young person will be very shortly concluded. It is merely to express my displeasure, and to express it with warmth such as I feel, that I have been imposed upon by you.
And that a worthy man has been imposed upon by you.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Brother, we have both done wrong, and both hope for pardon.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Amendment must precede forgiveness. She must return with her future husband.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Ah! Ah!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Oh, sir! did you know what it was to have a horror of being married!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Well,—well,—suppose I did know, what then?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Then, you wou'd pity me.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: The poor girl has a repugnance to marriage, and I compassionate her.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: For my part, brother, tho' I have taken this young lady in, yet I have lectured her.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: You “lecture her”—And by what authority have you lectured her?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Hah! you think nobody is to give lectures but yourself.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: How old are you?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I am near seventeen.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I shou'd not have thought you so much!

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: No: for not being used to fashionable company, I have nothing to say in conversation—except what I think.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Would to heaven all your sex had no more to utter.—The family in which you lived, your guardian, I suppose, used his influence to persuade you to marry?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Yes; and Mr. Willowear used his influence to persuade me too; but I had rather not.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I don't blame your being nice, and cautious in respect to marriage; but you should not have given your lover hopes.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I could not tell him to his face, that I hated him.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: But, you received his presents.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: It was the only favour I ever granted, and he asked a thousand.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Favours!

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: He called them so.—He said, he did not value the things he gave me, but for their being mine. Here is his great present of all—a diamond ring! —Will you have it? I shall give it with as much pleasure to you, as he gave it to me, I dare say— and shall think it a greater favour, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: This is a very singular girl you have introduced to me!

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: And I have introduced as singular a man to her —therefore, I trust, you will understand one another.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: For my part, she has taken my understanding away.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: And as, I believe, she herself never had any, you will agree better and better.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I shall take this ring, and return it to its first possessor.—And, now, as you intend to abandon him, and your former home, what do you design to do?
—Whither do you intend to go?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I did intend to stay here. But, I suppose, you wont suffer it; though Mrs. Sarah Mortland invited me, or I should not have made so free as to come.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Upon my word,—I only—

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Hush! Hold your tongue.—I want to hear her talk, not you.—And wou'd you be content to stay, and give up all your friends?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I hope, I shou'd find friends here.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: You have no parents?—no relations, I am told?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: My mother died, when I was an infant.—My father went abroad,—perhaps is dead too: I never knew any other relations, and I hardly know my own surname; for I am always called Hester.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: —A Mr. and Mrs. Ashdale brought you up?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: But were so unkind to me, that I durst not tell them I wou'dn't marry;—and, I hope, you will not send me back with a man I cannot love.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Then, you never lov'd him?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: O! no, no.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Nor ever lov'd any other man?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: O, no, never, never.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Nor ever could, I suppose?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.stage: (After looking at him, unconsciously, from head to foot.)
sp.p: Yes,—yes,—yes,—O, yes.—I think I cou'd.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I thought, you said, you had set your heart against marriage.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: No I have not.—No, no—but I should like to chuse my own husband.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: How choose? Women can't make love.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: But they can listen.—And I'll never listen, but where the sound is sweet.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Sweets are not always wholesome.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: And yet they preserve certain things, as well as vinegar.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I don't know how I can turn this girl out of the house. Poor creature!
She has lost her mother, and is not sure whether or no she has a father.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Then, do you be a father to her.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Is there such difference in our ages?—She's seventeen, and I am not above—

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: No; but I have been so used to hear you call yourself an old man—

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I beg your pardon, if I have—for that's making my elder sister a very old woman.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Well, and I shall have no objection to being an old woman, while it is a privilege of that state to be of service to the young ones.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: And you have been of great service to me—thank you—thank you.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Yes, sister—you are a very good woman, I believe; and if I do find fault with you, now and then, it is because I wish you to be my companion, and my companion to be as perfect as possible.— Yes, indeed—I think you have done quite right in sheltering this poor orphan—and I recommend her to your further protection.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: You'll dine with us, Sir Oswin?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Why, yes; I don't know that I am going any where—yes—I'll dine with you.
sp.stage: (Exeunt Mrs. Sarah and Hester. Hester curtsying low to Sir Oswin.)
sp.p: Poor girl! I really feel for her—poor girl!
sp.stage: (He walks about, moves the chairs and table—at last he takes up a book, sits down and reads—of a sudden he rises.)
sp.p: Yes, I'll see what can be done for this poor destitute girl. My sister, I dare say, can employ her in her domestic concerns.
sp.stage: (He sits down, and reads again; then takes his eye slowly from the book.)
sp.p: books my sure solace, and refuge from frivolous cares.—Books, the calmers, as well as the instructors of the mind.
sp.stage: (Looks in the book some time, then rises.)
sp.p: S'death! I cannot read. —What is the reason I cannot read?

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Well, Sir Oswin, have you seen her?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Yes,—I have seen her.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: And what do you think of my choice?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I think it a most imprudent one.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Why so?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Because she does not choose you.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Did she tell you so?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Has she not proved so?

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: I wish you wou'd let me see her.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: No, by no means.

I told you that if she could exculpate herself,—and in truth this has been the case.—Her promise to you, she avers, was given under the influence of fear.—She has flown to this house for protection; and I believe the laws of hospitality oblige me.—Here is your ring—But, as to the simple girl, without her own express desire, I cannot give up her.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Well, if you say so—But, I assure you, you are the only man to whom I shou'd choose to confide her.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: You don't confide her.—She came hither of her own accord—and one cannot, upon reflection, turn from one's door a human creature of whatever sex, whatever age.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: And hers, to be sure, is an interesting sex, as well as a tender age.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Which makes me the more concerned for her.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: And yet you used to be so severe, so hard upon the women.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: So I am still on women advanced in life; but one can't help having a sort of feeling for the young.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Did she part with the ring reluctantly?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: No; with as much pleasure as if it had been yourself.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: So, then, I must resign all hopes of her, I find.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: That's right.—And do so like a man.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: I must seek for some other object to divert my thoughts.—What pretty women have you hereabouts, to banish Hester from my mind?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: A number—a number.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Who are they? What are their names?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I cannot exactly count them all over by name.
Lady Susan Courtley, however, is among them, I know.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Is she here?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: I once paid my addresses to Lady Susan—I have a great mind to renew them.—If she consented, just now, it would take from the foolish, ridiculous figure I make, to be seen without a wife after being so near possessing one.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: She lives close by, at my uncle's.—She's on a visit there, and his house is but on the edge of my park. Come with me, and I'll shew you a short cut thro' the grounds.—And one of the pleasantest walks too! You can be there in a quarter of an hour.

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: Lavensforth discovered stretched on a Bank under a Tree—his black Servant kneeling by him—an open Letter lying on the Ground.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: Master, dear master, raise your head, and speak to poor servant, poor black, who has attend you from boy in his native country, followed you to your own, and is ready to follow all the world over.—Only tell him why you no eat—why you no sleep—and why big tear roll down from your eye?

Master, why you left lodgings in village, and taken this poor hut in wild forest? House, not fit for blacks.—No one live near—none but the birds.—Ah! forget—This letter he threw down brought the bad news that breaks his heart.
sp.stage: (Takes the letter from the ground, and reads.)
sp.p: “Unhappy man,—in all things unhappy—your daughter Hester, I fear is lost to you for ever.— She eloped from my care on the very day your packet arrived: and under such circumstances, that perhaps I may never hear of her again. If I do, I will certainly send her the letter you inclosed for her in mine.—Yours,“R. Ashdale.”Hester, that his daughter's name—often he talks of her, when in my country.—Hester—poor Hester!

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Who said “Poor Hester!” Ah! poor! for she lost her mother at her birth, and her father when she first began to know and love him. Did any one speak her name, or was it my imagination?

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: It was I said, Hester.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Wherefore?

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: Because I know that name well—You so often spoke it in your sleep, while, in hot countries, I watched to fan you.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Ah! my dreams have been happier than my waking hours; for them I passed with her.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: No, master, no—Your dreams sometimes unhappy! sometimes you start.—You angry in your sleep.—You call for gun, for sword.—You speak another name, not kind, as you speak Hester.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: I speak of Oswin, then, in my dreams.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: Ay; that's the name.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Of him, who has stript me of every good I once possess'd. Amos, I have a heart formed to love, and to hate in the extremes.—My daughter and this Oswin have, for thirteen years, shared it between them;—to the one, the tenderest affection; to the other, deadly hatred. And now, that I have no longer a child, on whom to bestow my love, hate is the sole possessor of my bosom. But I will root it out.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: Do, master, do.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: I have no daughter, for whose sake, now, I should retain my rage, and I will rid myself of it.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: You will forgive?

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: I will. There is, however, but one way left, by which I can forgive Sir Oswin, and I will avail myself of that one.—I will fix my dagger in his heart, and bear him malice no longer.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: Have duel?

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: No; from that redress, years ago, I was restrained; and the only friends I ever had on earth, are bound in penalties so large, to insure my forbearance, that I must steal upon him.—Amos, invention, plot, cunning, disguise, and secrecy must be employed, even to procure such a meeting. But, then,—Oswin, on my knees, I vow your destruction, as you have effected mine.

But my revenge shall be mercy, compared to yours.— I will not stab your fame:—I'll only sheathe my poniard in your breast.—I will not alienate your friends, as you have done mine; but they shall follow you with lamentation to the grave.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: Master, me commit that sin, not you. Me black, who been often wounded by white man, let me wound in return;—then sail to my own country, and leave master still good man,—no fear,—no guilt.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: You presume to complete my designs?— Avenge my wrongs?—Know your distance.—
sp.stage: (Then inattentive to him, as he has been through all the scene but where he particularly addressed him.)
sp.p: Good fortune might have softened my mind, and driven out all impressions of revenge.— But

the many ills which have succeeded his ambitious prosecution!—my child! a female child, left without parents, the heaviest ill of all.— His courting popularity at my expence! his art of eloquence, which, in a boy, had power to crush a man!—Of the miseries produced by talents so perverted, he shall feel his share:—He shall find I am not less cruel now, than when I ruled in my government; that exile has not softened me. The young enthusiast but accused me of acts of despotism; —he shall prove, in his dying moments, there is not a crime too black for my accomplishment.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: Good master, no more grief; but return to lodgings in the village.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: No house shall shelter me, but this ruin'd cottage; no bed shall rest my limbs, and rack my brain, till I have revenged my wrongs.
sp.stage: (Goes into the Cottage, returns and says at the door.)
sp.p: My enemy, this Sir Oswin Mortland, has a seat, not more than ten miles distant.—Mortland Abbey. —Inquire of the peasants what road he frequents; whether he passes this way to the next town; whether he hunts, or shoots, or strolls in his park of an evening.—Gain all the intelligence you can.— Revenge is dear to men of your complexion, even more than to those of mine. Therefore, I depend, not alone on your fidelity and secrecy, but on your eager exertions.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: Oh, master! only kind master I ever had.—I would die for your content.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Live—and execute my orders.

div.stage: (Lavensforth retires into the Cottage—and Amos into the Forest.)

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: —A Saloon at Lord Danberry's, with folding-doors into a Garden.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: There they are! there they are! Now would I give a hundred pounds, to know what Lady Susan and Sir Oswin are saying to each other.—They have been together exactly five minutes and a half by my stop-watch.— He has certainly begun the subject by this time; but I can't know any thing of their conversation, unless I join them—and that would be a pity, for it would interrupt them. I found it difficult to drag him to my house, and more so to persuade him to wait on her in the garden. Then, away I slipt—and now he is alone with her, he will be caught at once. He must speak now—here they come! here they come!—Yes, they are coming into this very room, as I live.—Now he must break the matter without delay, and my wishes are completed.

div.stage: Enter Sir Oswin and Lady Susan from the Garden.
(As he and Lady Susan sit down.)

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Lady Susan, I am a peculiar man, but a plain man: my peculiarity consists in my plainness. I am under the greatest obligations to my uncle, who bestowed on me an education, and tutors, who made me reflect—reflect particularly on my own passions, inclinations, faults, and failings.—In return for his care, I wish to obey him in all his commands—but, serious, sober, I'm afraid I may say, sullen habits, have ever been predominant with me; and I never was, and perhaps never shall be, in love.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Sir Oswin, your candour is so bewitching, it is impossible to resist its force. I have been accustomed to so much flattery, such adulation from men of the world, whose ardour, I am sure, meant nothing; that I cannot help believing—your apathy means a great deal.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: You may deceive yourself, Lady Susan.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: And so may you, Sir Oswin.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: As I observed before, Madam, self-examination has been my daily practice.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Perhaps you examine so frequently, that you weary penetration; and a passer-by knows you better than you know yourself.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: That observation, Madam, might hold true of a lady and her looking-glass; but not of a man and his faults!

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: He must, however, be a very bad man, Sir Oswin, who sees his faults thus daily, yet does not amend them.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: He will, at least, endeavour to shun all trials that he thinks beyond his strength; and, in that spirit, I fear a married life.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Marriage may be productive of some faults; but, surely, 'tis a soil fit for the cultivation of every virtue.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Patience, I believe, may thrive there.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: But what do you say of the growth of conjugal love?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: That conjugal hate too frequently chokes it.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: I long to convince you of your mistake.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Madam, to end the argument, and not to make my visit tedious—if you think you can be happy with a man so much older than yourself, who reads all the day, and half the night—whose temper is not good—who is easily put out of humour—

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: That I never am—therefore my good temper will make your fretful one of no harm to either of us!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I'll say no more, Madam.—My uncle will tell you the rest of my imperfections.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: They must all appear trivial, Sir Oswin, when compared with that sincerity which discloses them.

I am, you shall find, Sir, as peculiar, as plain spoken for a woman, as you are for a man.—I scorn, like you, to follow common modes and manners, which my own opinion, or my own convenience disapproves.—And while you have the singular frankness to tell me to my face, that you had rather not have me for a wife; I will adopt the same simple candour, and confess,—that, of all things, I should like you for a husband.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Good morning, Lady Susan.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Good morning, Sir Oswin.

div.stage: As Sir Oswin is going—Enter Lord Danberry.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Stay, my dear nephew, stay.—Nothing on earth could give me greater joy, than to be present at this interview. So, prolong it a little for my sake.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I am afraid of intruding.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Not at all, Sir Oswin. The man, who has honour'd me with the offer of his hand—

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Then the offer is made, and you are his betrothed wife.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: As you have previously told me, my Lord; but Sir Oswin has said very little.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Talking is not his talent; that is, talking to you women; for he thinks that would be encroaching on your privileges:—when he speaks, 'tis for nothing less than the good of the nation.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: If I may judge of his other virtues by his humility, he will make the best husband in the world; for he assures me he shall be the worst.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: My uncle knows, Madam,—

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: I know that you are a good man, and, therefore, will make a good husband;—you were the most dutiful son,—you are an affectionate nephew,—a good brother,—a staunch friend,—a friend to the orphan; for that pretty girl, whom you have just taken into your house,—how kindly I saw you look on her.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: What pretty girl?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: A child, Madam,—a mere child.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Nothing the worse for being young,—nor the worse for her beauty.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Is she so beautiful, Sir Oswin?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I was going to say, I had never look'd at her; —but I did,—I did.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Who is she? What's her name?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I never ask'd:—she was friendless, I heard.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: And well she might; for she ran from all her friends, and the man to whom she was going to be married, at the church-door.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: What a surprising occurrence!

sp.speaker: SIR OWSIN.
sp.p: And yet I can conceive it might happen.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: But the best of the story is, (as her guardian has written just now to Mr. Willowear,) she persuaded a second lover of hers, to hire the post-chaise for her escape from the first, on a promise she would go off with him; but, as they were stepping into the vehicle, she pretended to swoon; and, while the poor man ran for a smelling bottle, she drove away, and left both her lovers in the same deserted state.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Can this be fact?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Mr. Willowear but now shewed it under her guardian's hand; who adds,—he believes she will, in the end, prefer this second lover.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Who is he? What's his name?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: He did not say.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: 'Tis fit, however, I shou'd search into the truth of this story, before she remains longer in my house.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Nay, don't put yourself in a passion with her— don't go home on purpose—don't leave Lady Susan.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: If it be proper to order Hester away, the sooner she knows my will, the better.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Then send a message to your sister; my own man shall take it, and see her safe off, at once.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: No; she shall not go, till she has received from my own lips, the reproof she deserves, for having dared to come.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Why, then Lady Susan and I will go with you. Lady Susan, we'll go with my nephew.

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: Mr. Willowear.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Pray, Mr. Willowear,—But, no,—I'll talk to Hester herself.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Nephew, nephew!—one word.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Lady Susan, I did myself the honour of waiting on your Ladyship yesterday; but you were not within.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: O! yes—I think they told me so.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Hearing your Ladyship was in this part of the world, I came to confess my shame. I knew it would be impossible to conceal it from you, and I wished to be the first to announce it. I have been slighted in the most public manner, by one of your sex, to whom I paid my addresses, in consequence of their having been rejected by you.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: She used you rightly, if you only made your offer on my refusal.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: But, then, are not you bound to take pity on me now, if my attachment to you has ruin'd me with every other woman?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: You don't mean this seriously, I hope, Mr. Willowear; because Sir Oswin—

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: My Lord, let Sir Oswin speak for himself.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I can't think of interrupting my uncle, Madam.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Why, then, Mr. Willowear, this lady is engaged to Sir Oswin, and will shortly be his wife; and let me tell you, Sir—

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: My Lord, how can you be so warm?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Sir Oswin, how can you be so cold?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: My Lord—

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Don't interrupt your uncle, Sir Oswin.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: I beg ten thousand pardons; but it was Sir Oswin, who first told me Lady Susan was here. And I understood—

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: You can't misunderstand any longer now, Sir.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Upon my honour, I think I do—for Sir Oswin's going to be united to Lady Susan, is the most surprising!—Sir Oswin!—who has always protested there was no such thing as love.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: But I never denied there was matrimony.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: What a prospect for me in the marriage state! But I'll be revenged for his chilling insolence; and nothing on earth shall make me resign him.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: That's right, my proud woman!

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Lady Susan, I admire your spirit so much, that I have a great mind to say,—nothing on earth shall make me resign you.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Would you supplant Sir Oswin, Mr. Willowear? Is it friendly?

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: 'Tis fashionable.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Will you, my Lord, insist on Sir Oswin's promise, given to you?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: I will;—I do insist upon it.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Then I'll force him to marry me.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Do—and force him to love you too.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: So I will.—For I'll bear his cruelty with so much good humour, that, unless his heart be more frozen than his manners, it shall beat with warmth to me.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Stay, Lady Susan—take pity on the only man who loves you—do not drive me to despair.
My Lord, can you tell me of any other woman, whom you think I could love?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Why, upon my word, Mr. Willowear, it seems, as if you could love every woman you saw.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: I own I am not difficult; but, I find they are so.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: My advice is, pursue Hester—try to redeem her; and if you do not succeed—
I have just thought of the very female, who will exactly suit you.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Of perfectly good character, I hope?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: The nicest?

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Family?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: The very best in the country.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Fortune?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Better than Lady Susan's.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: When will you introduce me?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: I'll mention the subject to her first, and settle every thing between you both, as I have settled between Sir Oswin, and Lady Susan.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: But that aliance does not appear to be quite settled yet—I hope you will be more successful for me.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: I'll be successful for you all. But, before I undertake your affairs, you must come with me to Sir Oswin's, and try to regain Hester.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: My Lord, I am of an easy, complying, satisfied disposition.—I am willing to marry Hester; or Lady Susan; or the unknown female you propose; or, if she does not like me, some other.—I am not one of those, who think “great care must be taken in the choice of a wife, that she may prove a blessing.”

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: No, say with me—“great care must be taken how you treat a wife, and she will certainly be a blessing.”

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: Enter Roberts, James, Harry, and John, Servants to Sir Oswin.

sp.speaker: ROBERTS.
sp.p: Do you run to the terrace, and see for her.
Go you, and see if she's in the drawing-room.
And run you into the park.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: What is the matter? What is all this confusion about?

sp.speaker: ROBERTS.
sp.p: I thought Miss Hester was here, Ma'am.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: And what did you want with her?

sp.speaker: ROBERTS.
sp.p: Sir Oswin is just returned from Lord Danberry's, and desires to see her directly.—He seems not very well pleas'd at something.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: You mean, he is in an ill humour.

sp.speaker: ROBERTS.
sp.p: He's coming, Ma'am.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Where is your protègée, your companion, your innocent girl? Where's Hester?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: And, now, give me leave to ask a question. Where is your elder sister? For one would suppose she was not within hearing.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: She lost her consequence, when she listen'd to the tale of an impostor.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: What has thus changed you on a sudden? We passed yesterday in comfort all together—and your attention to this poor girl, was remarkable.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Who remarked it?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Myself—Lord Danberry.—However, do you want to see her?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I do.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Then I'll send her to you—
and glad of the opportunity to get away.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Women!—women!—women!—
woman! woman! woman!
woman!

sp.stage: (His voice softens, as he beholds her, and he tenderly pronounces)
sp.p: woman!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: If they were slight faults you had committed, you would see me in anger— as it is—as your indiscreet conduct has been flagrant —you find me impressed only with concern, that I am compelled to turn from my habitation, a friendless young woman, who had implored my protection—and afflicted—deeply afflicted—to behold depravity in one, who gave no warning to the eye, no caution to the ear, nor even to the understanding, to beware of her arts.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Am I artful? If you say so, I suppose I am; but, indeed, I did not know it.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Were not those arts, by which you deceived two lovers?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: O! lovers! Yes, I have made fools of two lovers. But I had a right to do so—for they wanted to make a fool of me.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: How so?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Why, Mrs. Ashdale, my guardian's wife, and all the elderly ladies, that visited her, constantly said to me, “Hester, never mind what the men say; they are deceitful, and always speak falsehood to young women.”—So, I put no trust in them, nor they, I hope, in me.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: One honourable man was on the point of marrying you, when you ran away.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I thought it was better to run away before marriage, than after.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: But you broke your promise.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Not my marriage-promise—for that I am resolved to keep, marry when I will—
which makes me so afraid of giving it.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: That is from the heart.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Have you any thing more to say against me?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Who was he that effected your escape?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I did not know him for a lover; but trusted him only as a friend, to procure me a chaise; when, on a sudden, thinking me in his power, he wanted to come away with me.—So, I feigned illness, to leave him behind, too.—Any more reproaches?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Numberless. You have, in every instance, conducted yourself with so much imprudence, indecorum, —that I am offended you shou'd have dared to come into this house.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Ay, now I hope you are speaking falsehood, as all the men do to young women.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I speak falsehood!

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Only to women—don't be angry—I mean, only to women.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I speak truth to every one;—and it is true that you have forfeited my good opinion, and all that favourable impression, which your appearance first made on me.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Did I make a favourable impression on you? Oh! I am so proud of it!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I—I give you leave to conceive this as a falsehood.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: No:—you always “speak truth;”—and I will believe this true, because I should be sorry to have it otherwise:—for then, what would become of me? Where should I go?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Return to those who reared you from your infancy.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: No, no, never.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Marry, and you'll have a home.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Why do you bid me marry? I am told that you don't like to marry any more than I do.— But, sir,—is not this a fair proposal?—I'll marry, if you will.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Mr. Willowear, would you marry?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: No; I'll make my own choice.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: And whom would you choose?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I'll tell you, if you'll promise I shall have him.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Hear me, Hester—I sent for you, to upbraid, to reproach you—to shew my displeasure—my resentment;—but, you talk so differently from all the world besides, that—that— I have no words to give in exchange for yours, but such as I feel disinclined to utter.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Are they cruel, or kind words that you suppress?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I hardly know their meaning.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Speak them, and I'll explain them.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: No, no;—no explanations.—

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: And, now, if my examination is over, am I to stay or go?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I am not determined.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Shall I determine for you?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: I confess, since the conversation which has just past between us, I feel a reluctance to say those harsh things, I meant to do, before I saw you.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: We feel something alike; for, before we met, I intended to say a thousand kind things, to persuade you to let me remain here; but the moment I saw you, I was ashamed to speak them.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: It is not discreet in a woman, to speak with kindness to men.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Not if they speak kindly to her: but when they are cross, like you, she may be kind with safety.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Hester, with all your faults, I feel an interest in your welfare.—And when I say, I feel for another's happiness, I am not interested slightly.—You have been imprudent, and I have censured you—but, in the hope my censure may have influence, I commence, from this hour, a friendship—a sincere friendship for you. Remain in this house while it suits your convenience, and reveal to me all your heavy sorrows, all your anxious troubles—my power shall protect, my sympathy shall console you.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.stage: (After pausing a little time, impressed with surprize.)
sp.p: Oh! this serious, this solemn profession of regard for me, has ruined all my hopes, all my expectations!

sp.speaker: OSWIN.
sp.p: How so? How?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Because it forces me to be serious and solemn with you. While you were proud, I could treat you lightly;—while you were angry, I did not regard you;—while you were severe, I could laugh at you.—But now you are generous, humble, mild, I cannot impose on you—cannot deceive you longer.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Deceive me! In what? Don't I know all your faults?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Not half of them.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Have a care! you may yet lose me as your friend.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I may—Oh, I must!—I know I must!—I shall not make my confession unwarily; for I know, the moment you have heard it we shall part, never to meet again. Yet, I had rather it shou'd be so, than live with you every day, and be ashamed to lift up my eyes in your presence.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Why ashamed?—Why are you to be excluded from the right, which every one who is friendless has to my protection?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Because I am the unhappy child— of the unfortunate Lavensforth.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: My enemy! my mortal enemy! The man who has threatened, who has repeatedly sworn to take my life!
sp.stage: (She falls gradually on her knees, as he speaks thus to himself.)
sp.p: The man whom my rigour has irritated to this phrenzy! Ay, Oswin, reason for your foe, as well as for yourself.—Act, too, for him.
I do not discard you for your father's sake; and you shall be still nearer to me for your own.
Nay, why this trembling, this tremour?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Wherefore am I thus impelled, thus forced to love the man who was my father's enemy?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: If I continued such, I would not offend you with the offer of my services.—But time and reflection have made me doubt of his demerits, and my own justice in arraigning him.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Ah! do you say so? Do I hear there is a doubt —a supposition—a hope, that my dear father has been unjustly accused?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: From his open, his once profest enemy, his daughter shall receive his character; and before she blesses—honours—my abode with her future residence, know—that I respected the man whom I impeached; for esteem was not incompatible with that peculiar suit I preferred against him. And, now, while compassion suggests numerous excuses for his past deeds—and impartiality obliges me to reprove my own,—do you, his representative, accept all the retribution I can offer for measures too severe, perhaps, in the cause of political warfare.
sp.stage: (He takes her hand, and holds her tenderly in his arms.)

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Ah! what! my rigid, reserved nephew, with a fair maid in his arms! Oh! you can unbend, I find, serene and mighty potentate, when no one is by.

Madam, Mr. Willowear is in the next room, come to claim you—you blush!—but never mind—I won't tell—mum!—For my part, Sir Oswin, I am rather glad to see that you can get a pretty girl in a corner; for if you do one, you soon may another; and Lady Susan, perhaps, has no cause to despair.—Mum!—hush!—I won't say a word—only I must laugh—ha! ha! ha!—Is this the lesson you came home to give the poor orphan? ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: My Lord, you—

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: No excuses—'tis all very well—only give a little of your kindness to Lady Susan.—I thought it wou'd shew itself at last!

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Sir—

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: No excuses, my dear—I forgive—no excuses.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: My Lord, you put me in a rage!

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Ay, the cold fit has been gone some time.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: My Lord, Sir Oswin was so kind—

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: You need not tell me.—I saw how kind he was!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Hold!—that lady must not be insulted—she is under my protection.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Well, this is leaping from the “freezing point” to “fever heat” at once! One moment in Lapland, the next under the torrid zone! I wish you joy, young lady, of this your third lover; but, perhaps, I shou'd not be so content, if a fourth was not behind.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: A fourth lover!

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Yes; her guardian has just sent a post-chaise (at least a messenger, who was to procure one, if he found her here) to take her to a fourth lover, who may, perhaps, extinguish your burning flame.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Oh! Sir Oswin, save me from my guardian, and his tyranny.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: But if your guardian possesses any power, any authority, I have no legal right to withhold you.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: But, you may have.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: There,—she speaks as plain English, as ever I heard a woman utter.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Plain English is what so few of the English do speak,—

div.stage: Enter Mrs. Sarah Mortland, with two Letters in her hand.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Hester,—
sp.stage: [when Mrs. Sarah calls out “Hester,” Lord Danberry passes by Sir Oswin towards Hester.]
sp.p: Here is a letter for you, which came inclosed in this to me; and there's a person from your guardian, who begs to see you instantly.
sp.stage: (Mrs. Sarah retires a little reading her own letter.)

div.stage: Hester receives her Letter, looks at the address with joy and surprize, and kissing it, exclaims apart.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: My father's hand! Oh, unexpected happiness!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Her guardian! What can all this mean?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: I must have an eye upon this girl. She must not belong to my family;
I must watch her.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: You are absorbed in thought! May I ask what is the subject of your reflections?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: A confused mass! I am living in this old world, and yet a new one seems to have broken upon me, to make me as a stranger to all around.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Shall I inform you, where you are?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: It would be an act of charity.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: But will you take it charitably?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: You are—in love.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: What makes you think so?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Don't you feel so?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: No,—no,—no,—let's hope not,—no—no.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: You have all the symptoms.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: No—no.—And who made you a judge?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: That is a secret I shall keep to myself.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Women, to be sure, know every thing.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: The reason is—women feel every thing. Men's perception lies only in the head; ours comes from the heart. Brother, the two sexes are thus contrasted —Sensibility gives us wisdom, but takes it away from you men. When man is governed by his heart, he's less than woman—and we are the lords of the creation.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: In this case neither my heart nor head convicts me.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: No; for they dupe you.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Do you speak in earnest?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Most assuredly.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Why, then, if I am in love,—if it must be so,—I may as well submit.

It is vain, I suppose, to contend with my passion, and I must give myself up to my fate? Hard fate! after all my studies, my researches, my meditations, my zeal for the public good! And what am I to do in respect to Lady Susan?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: You must tell her you prefer another.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: If I told her I was married to another, she would say she liked me the better for it
. Hester is different from her: she has a horror of the marriage state.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: So, from the self-same antipathy arises this dangerous sympathy. But as I allured you into her power, it is my duty to snatch you from it This letter was just now brought me from her guardian.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: “Madam, do me the favour to give Hester the inclosed, the contents of which she is bound to keep secret. All I shall add is, that you can, upon no pretence whatever, detain her longer, when I assure you, that this inclosed letter comes to her from one, who (as I have acquainted him with her flight) must be in the deepest despair till he sees her; as there is between them a mutual and indissoluble affection.” “A mutual affection!”
Yes, I observed her delight on seeing the hand which directed her letter.—'Tis true, she has a secret lover, and I will search him out, or—

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Now this, is jealousy.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Jealous! do you accuse me of love, and then dare to add jealousy?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: They follow naturally.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Why, then, welcome to all the tumultuous passions at once; for I find my heart is as unable to resist the one as the other.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Ah! I foresaw—

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Why did you not caution me, then? why did you not tell me? I felt no fears—I despised all danger—
Why did you ever bring her to my house? Or, rather, why not long since? For, till I knew her, I never knew one rapturous sensation.

div.stage: Enter Hester, with a letter in her hand.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I am come to take leave of you for ever.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Why so?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I must not tell you why.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: And do you go by your own consent?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I do.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Then wherefore do you weep?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Half these tears are for joy, half for sorrow.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Explain.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I dare not; but must follow my guardian's directions, and immediately set off in the carriage, which his servant, who brought this letter, is gone to procure me.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Alone?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: All alone.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Not an hour ago you solicited me to save you from your guardian's power.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: But I was not then acquainted with the cause, which—Oh! Sir Oswin, an impulse you know nothing of compels—and the same impulse (confident as I am in your nice honour) ties my tongue from saying what the occasion is, which calls me.— All my own actions—all my own thoughts, I confess boldly; but when I am entrusted with the thoughts and the concerns of others, I can be mute as death.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: You are going to a lover.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: No more—than I am leaving one behind.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: And if you thought, you were—?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Have I any right to think so?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Do you ask me seriously?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Why, then, I—

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: The chaise waits—the postillion's in a hurry.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Oh dear! how could you interrupt what he was going to say?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Hear what I have to say—The chaise is at the door—'twill be dark in half an hour—no moon— the common you have to cross is dangerous, on account of robbers—and the rivulet, at the bottom of the hill, has, probably, overflowed.
Here's your hat and cloak.—
sp.stage: (He takes them of her, and gives them to Hester.)
sp.p: I sincerely wish you a good journey, and I'll hand you to the door.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: No, uncle, as the danger is so great, I'll order my horse, and pistols, and ride by the side of the chaise. It wou'd not be common hospitality to suffer a female to leave my house, unprotected, through such perils as you have described.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: You must not go with me, for the world—not for the world, Sir Oswin.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: This alarm is suspicious!—What does it mean?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Dear Mrs. Sarah Mortland, persuade your brother —my Lord do not suffer him to go with me.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: These efforts to prevent me, fix my determination.
To see her meeting with her lover, will be my cure at once.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: I hope that, when I have passed the dangerous part of my journey, I shall have power to persuade you to return.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Perhaps, you may.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: If not, I must reveal to whom I am going.

sp.speaker: LORD. DAN.
sp.p: Nephew—nephew!
You had a fixed opinion there was no such passion as love.—What can you say now?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Like other theorists, say—I was mistaken.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Did you ever see any thing like this?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Yes; for this is not the first time I have seen a man in love.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: My dear Willowear, did you not meet Sir Oswin, leading away in triumph your intended wife? Run after him, and take her from him; pray now do.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: No—let Hester go—and let Lady Susan go.— I am curious and impatient to see the woman you have promised me.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: You shan't see her; nor will I reveal who she is, till you have followed Sir Oswin.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Then I'll make enquiries elsewhere.
sp.stage: (Bows to Mrs. Sarah, and goes up to her.)
sp.p: I beg pardon, madam; but, as I have the honour to meet you in the house of Sir Oswin, I imagine you know the name of Willowear
; and know that he has met with a certain disappointment?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: I do, Sir.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: I am that unfortunate lover.—Can you, madam, give me advice how to repair my loss? Do you know any woman of reputation who will marry a man in my forsaken state.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Upon my word, I am so little acquainted with any, except the married women of our neighbourhood! —I assure you, Mr. Willowear, I have hardly an acquaintance who is a single lady, although I am single myself.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Are you unmarried, madam?
Who is this lady? I was never introduced to her.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: She is Sir Oswin's sister—my niece—and the very woman I mentioned for your wife.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: My wife! my wife!

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: No fear of running away from the church-door, there.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Marry her!—I should be the jest of all my acquaintance.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: That you will be, at any rate.
