sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Mine is a desperate case.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: And, to tell you the truth, I don't believe that even she would accept you.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Now you pique me to make the offer.
Madam, you are Mrs. Sarah Mortland, I find.
If I thought you would pardon what I am inclined to utter—

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Pray speak out, Sir.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Will you, accept a man, slighted by all your sex?

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Would you marry a woman, who has been slighted by all yours?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: To be sure:—for then you can't laugh at each other.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: If you could, Mr. Willowear, marry such a woman, I give you in reply—that at my time of life, I feel for every man the same disregard, the men all felt for me in my younger days.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: What can I do now, my lord? Will you—

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: No—I can do no more—After being refused by a maiden lady of fifty, all hope is over.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Nay, hear me, my lord.—Oh! that I had but Sir Oswin's aversion to matrimony.

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: —The Forest and Cottage as in Act III.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: How seldom do we taste the goods, which nature bestows, till we are deprived of those that are the work of art. To see the sun set, and the moon rise, is to me, robbed of every other pastime, sublime delight! And were fortune now to shower on me all its wealth, and other hoarded blessings, still I should ever think—Hark! what noise?— Amos, returning from the village!—perhaps with letters.—The thought of news makes me shudder; for 'tis so many years since I have received good tidings!—Still I send, and long for letters.—But, now, what intelligence can they bring me, except the confirmation of my Hester's loss.—Hark! again!—That sound was like a groan!—No; —my own dark designs, my own black determinations haunt me, and, in every whisper of the wind through these lofty oaks, I hear the cry of murder.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Ho! ho! Cottagers, lend assistance!

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Who's there in distress? Amos, is it you? Speak again, that I may know which way the sound—

div.stage: Enter Sir Oswin, pale and near fainting.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Good friend, a villain on the road has fired at me—

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Ha! who's that? Who are you?—You are wounded, Sir—lean on me.— Come into this cottage. Let me bind your wounds.
sp.stage: (Tearing a neckcloth from his own neck.)
sp.p: Then haste for other assistance, and raise the village in pursuit of the robber.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: He is fled—I have rode a mile, at least, since I received my wound; for my horse took fright at the report of the piece, and I had no power over him, till he was stopped by this wood.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: If you can walk into the cottage, it will be better than—

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: There is a lady in a carriage, with whom I was in company, whose safety is more important to me than my own.—She was under my protection.— Lead me into the house—then, my good friend, go in search of her; silence her fears, and order the post-boy to drive hither; he can take me home.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Here is, in this hut, a kind of couch, on which you may rest, when I have bound up your wound: I will then instantly do as you have directed.—Lean on me; I can support you,—Your blood flows fast. —Do not talk, I charge you—it will exhaust you quite.—But lean on me—lean on me—lean on me.

div.stage: [Exit, drawing Sir Oswin gently into the cottage.
Enter Amos (in great fright and terror, a firelock in his hand).

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: Master! master! Where is he?
sp.stage: (Looks slightly into the cottage window, and about.)
sp.p: Cannot find him!—away!—is not to be found—I, left to feel joy!
and sorrow alone! Ah! cannot bear, alone.—Master—master.—Come—I happy with you—but what, what do, if ever left alone!

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: What's all this talking? Fly instantly for the village surgeon.—Here is a gentleman within, has been wounded by some villain, who fired at him on the road.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: Here?—here?

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Yes, here.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.stage: (With expression of joy and savage fury.)
sp.p: It is Sir Oswin.
It is Sir Oswin.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: You speak falsehood.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: Master, it is he.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: No; such joy, such triumph, was never meant for me. Yet the sound pleases me—repeat it—say again, it is he.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: I know it.—As, I returning, from the village— this gun in hand,—which had lately borrowed,— heard carriage stop on road, and postilion enquire his way—I answered to him—on which—lady from chaise-window said to gentleman on horseback— “Now, Sir Oswin, you go no further.” I start at that name—went close to horses' side, and asked— if he was Sir Oswin Mortland, of Mortland Abbey. He answered “Yes.” My hand, before my thought, caught trigger of my gun, and—
His horse ran away—I came home.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Strike a light.
I'll look at him as he reclines on his couch—I shall know him.
sp.stage: (A light appears at the cottage window, Amos re-enters.)
sp.p: I have cause to know him.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: Ah! I again alone! Nobody to speak—all to think—thoughts bad company—good company once—Oh! I cannot—cannot live, if I am alone.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: 'Tis he; 'tis he! the lineaments of his face are neither altered by time, nor the loss of blood. The man who has injured me bears the same features, thank Providence! as in the days of his malignant triumph. There can be no mistake—my eye, my heart, my very soul, recognizes the man. Ah! never more will I arraign just fate, who now has sent my worst enemy under my roof
, and wounded to my hand.—

Under my roof, and wounded to my hand!—why then I must not harm a hair of his head!—my limbs are chained, though my revenge is raging to burst forth. Oh! would he now start up in health and vigour, surrounded by his host of friends, how boldly would I defy, and stab him to the heart. But this good fortune, these secure means of vengeance, which every sculking coward would enjoy, I, bound by a tyrannical word, called honour, dare not use.

div.stage: Enter Sir Oswin from the cottage.
(Exit Amos, drooping under confusion and remorse at his presence.)

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: My good host, you have bound my wound so effectually, that the bleeding is wholly stopt; and I find my strength so well recruited by this short repose, that I hope the injury I have sustained will prove but slight.—As the chaise I mentioned is not come, if you can help me to my horse, who, probably, is still about this thicket, I shall thank you.—I am Sir Oswin Mortland,
, and if you'll call to-morrow at my house—
Ah! an instrument of death in your hand! Have I been betrayed into this place? What mean you by that weapon?

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: I mean, that it shall rest here,
till you are safe at home.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Till I am safe at home!—What then?—

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Then—it shall still rest, till your health is restored.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: You seem to imply some menace.—Man, who are you?

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Your sworn, your mortal, your just enemy— Lavensforth.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: You know the penalty under which the laws forbid my meeting you: that consideration, I am now compelled to wave, and to tell you—I have still strength and spirit to defy your threats.—
Choose one of these, and take your ground.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.stage: (Takes a pistol, then, seeming to make an effort.)
sp.p: No,—mean as this habitation is, proud man, it is mine—and you shall feel the weight of my protection,
while you are within its precincts.

sp.speaker: AMOS.
sp.p: A lady,—a lady, call for Sir Oswin.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN
sp.p: Your conduct towards me, is that of a generous foe,—
sp.stage: (Enter Hester, leaning on Amos—Exit Amos into the cottage)
sp.p: —and merits a return like this,
to prove me worthy of it.—Lavensforth, your daughter.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: My daughter! my daughter in your care!

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: If you are Lavensforth, I am your child.
Your once-loved Hester,— most unkindly treated by those friends, with whom you trusted me, and sheltered from misfortune by—

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: My enemy!

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: No; my father, the defender of your fame, and his own accuser, in all the conversations he has had with me, when your misfortunes were the subject. Then, do not rob him of the praise due to his pity for a hapless female,—who owes to him her preservation to this blissful meeting.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: The tender joy I feel, in thus pressing you to my bosom, hushes every murmur of resentment. “My enemy!” no—the man, who has sheltered thee, to bless my age, to soothe the rancourous passions of my soul! The man, who could preserve you, my child, from sorrow, however he has dealt with me, shall, henceforth, be my friend.

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Oh, then, my father, your daughter's joy for your return is perfect.
sp.stage: (They embrace, and shew other tokens of affection.)

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: How poor was my exultation, while I urged on the ruin of this man, compared to the delight the present moment gives me!

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: No forethought, no calm consideration, could restrain me from a first embrace;—but, before I indulge, too far, my parental love, clear your late conduct from your guardian's accusation.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Lavensforth, I would not have presented her to you, as a boon, had I not believed she was a blessing, such as I would, joyfully, receive from you.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: My dear child! my dearest Hester!—Oh! supreme must be my happiness, when I can feel it undisturbed, even by the presence of Sir Oswin.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Suffer me to participate in your happiness! Suffer me,—
Excess of interest, vehement emotions of the mind have supplied me with strength to—but now, again—

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Ah! you have been wounded!—Where is the carriage? Instantly return home.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Order the carriage here— to this very spot—and return instantly.
Sir Oswin, before you and I part, you must be told—Come hither—
—It was this man, my servant, from whom you received your wound—
instigated by my thirst, my plans of vengeance, but not encouraged by my most distant concurrence, or suspicion of his guilty design.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: You have more cause to rejoice at the preservation of my life, than I have—you have escaped greater peril than myself.—I'll pardon you, when time shall have proved your repentance.

div.stage: (Amos rises, and goes into the cottage, overwhelmed with shame; Sir Oswin is between Lavensforth and Hester, holding the hand of each.—In gestures he earnestly entreats them to accompany him home. They go off apparently with this design.)

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter Mrs. Sarah, meeting Lady Susan.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Dear Lady Susan, I sent for you, both to console me, and share my grief! My poor brother is, perhaps, this moment breathing his last.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Oh, heavens!

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: He went out on horseback, and was attacked by robbers.—The servant, who was following at a distance, and saw him wounded, returned home, supposing his master was come back also; as he perceived him ride down a bye road leading this way. —But Sir Oswin not having returned, I fear his wounds may be mortal, and he—

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Is my Lord yet informed—

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: No; and I have sent the servants all about, in vain, to seek him.—Oh! my Lord will die with grief when he hears the news—and I am so anxious to tell him.—

div.stage: Enter Mr. Willowear, on the opposite side—Lady Susan turns complaisantly to him, and makes a kind salute or curtsy.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: How do you do, Mr. Willowear?

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: To see Lady Susan smile upon me, is good fortune, so extraordinary!—a smile, too, when, if report says true, her favour'd lover is dying.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: The favourite lover of a woman of fashion, Mr. Willowear, has the same prerogative as a king,—he never dies—there's always an immediate successor.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Could I be that happy man?

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Yes: I'll make you heir apparent to my hand; but while Sir Oswin lives, he is its lawful sovereign.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Nay, promise you will be mine, before you know his fate.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: No; I must delay plighting my faith, 'till I know whether poor Sir Oswin lives, or dies.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: That will depreciate its value. Come, give me your promise now.—You can break it, you know.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: Very true; I forgot that.—Then I promise.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: And thus humbly I take your word.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Heyday! What in the name of wonder is this? More couples in corners? What do you mean, Mr. Willowear?—Why, where's my nephew?

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Do you think, my Lord, no man can be favour'd by a lady, except your nephew?

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: He is far off, my Lord, and, I fear, does not think of me.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: I am a very unfortunate personage! I can take no step, turn myself no way, but I intrude upon somebody's private hours. Pray, is this a concerted plan?

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: How concerted? What do you mean?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Why, it seems to me, as if you, Mr. Willowear with my nephew's intended bride—and he, with yours—were all going down a country dance, and that each had resolved to take the wrong partner.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: I think myself happy to have any partner at all.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: And suppose we have changed partners, my lord, what then?

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Why, then?—I feel myself like a blind fidler, whose instrument has put every one in motion, only to make 'em change sides.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: Oh, my lord, I am so glad I have found you! Have not you heard that Sir Oswin has been attacked by robbers, and, perhaps, is dying?

div.stage: Enter Sir Oswin, Lavensforth, Hester,—Servants attending them.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: “My nephew—robbers—dying!”—

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: No, my lord, I am still living—but my life has been in danger, and was preserved by the hospitality of this stranger.—

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: From henceforth, then, I am that stranger's friend.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: And we have agreed that I shall be so too,— and he mine—though his name once indicated my mortal enemy.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: “Enemy!” You never had an enemy, except Lavensforth.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: Now, then, he has not one.—

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: Is it possible this can be Lavensforth?

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: It is.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: And is it possible that such a reconciliation has taken place?

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Can you ask the question in a Christian country? —To forgive—is the peculiar virtue, the supreme criterion of our sacred religion. We, once, were deadly foes—This embrace
is the confession, the bold confession of our faith.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: We have hated as men, not reflecting on man's infirmities,—but presuming to expect divine perfections, cloathed in human clay.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: To speak in the same phrase, has not this little piece of earth helped to effect the wonderful change? Is she not of the same soil with him?

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: She is my daughter, and was given to me by Sir Oswin, when I thought her lost.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: I have no notion how all this has been accomplished! But that I shall learn hereafter, I suppose. —And now, Mr. Lavensforth, I verily believe, that the only recompense you can make my nephew for his gift, is to return her back again.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: If you do, Lavensforth, and Hester comes willingly, I will endow her with my heart, and protect her with my life.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: And will you go to church again, young lady?

sp.speaker: HESTER.
sp.p: Yes; and shall remember, with more joy than ever,—that I once ran away from it.

sp.speaker: LAVENSFORTH.
sp.p: And, now, you possess all that is dear to me, Sir Oswin, what mighty compensation you have in your power, for my past afflictions!

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: And will Sir Oswin stoop from his solemn, stately grandeur, to be married at last? Ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Not only to marry; but to marry, for love—Ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN, WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: Mr. Willowear—Lady Susan,—I should have apologies to make for some parts of my conduct to both of you; but I allow you the privilege of laughing at me; and I'm sure you'll think that a sufficient atonement.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: Sir Oswin, you are perfectly welcome to that Lady, as Lady Susan has given her promise to take me at last.

sp.speaker: LADY SUSAN.
sp.p: But I can break it, you know, Mr. Willowear.

sp.speaker: WILLOWEAR.
sp.p: But you won't, you know, Lady Susan.

sp.speaker: LORD DAN.
sp.p: As I said just now, you are all set to cross partners. —But I consent—and pray heaven that marriage may prove to each couple a merry tune; and none of you, ever make a false step in the dance.

sp.speaker: MRS. SARAH.
sp.p: But now, gentlemen, and ladies, if it was me, I wou'dn't delay, but marry to-morrow: for you are all such slippery kind of people, I'm afraid you should yet glide from each other's grasp.

sp.speaker: SIR OSWIN.
sp.p: That would be a prospect of more terror to me, than ever matrimony was—For, the passion I once derided, now repays itself for my scorn, and forces me thus openly to declare—That there certainly is such a tender power, such a rapturous influence, as —Love—And, that every man, who feels, like me, its genuine force, should—marry.
